title: Linux distributions: families, life cycles and choosing one

videos.script: The server in the cupboard runs Ubuntu. When Ana mentions that it will need replacing one day, three people give her three answers. A friend who programs says Fedora. A forum says Arch. The accounting software's vendor says their product is certified on Red Hat Enterprise Linux and nothing else. {{answers}} All four are Linux. They share the same kernel, and most of the same commands. So what exactly is being chosen? {{same}} A distribution is somebody's decision about everything around the kernel: which tools come with it, how software is installed, where it is downloaded from, how often a new version comes out, and for how many years somebody keeps fixing the old one. {{around}} In this lesson you will ask a Linux machine which distribution it is and where it came from, see how distributions form families that share a package tool, compare fixed releases with rolling ones, read how long a release is supported, and choose one for a job rather than for a taste. {{steps}} Every transcript comes from the Ubuntu server of lesson 3. The other distributions are described, not run. {{honest}}
